item.title: Things I Learned in 2025
item.description:
With 2025 behind us, the numbers look bleak. My five-year average for “Things I Learned” is 61 factoids, but last year fewer than 20 items made it onto the list. Not to worry, though: 2026 is on track to return to the greatness of yore.

  1. That white stuff in your cheese? It might be neither mold nor salt crystals 🧀

    Different cheeses form different crystals. Aged cheddar and Gouda often develop calcium lactate crystals on the surface as calcium salts migrate and recrystallize. Washed-rind cheeses may show salt crystals from surface treatments. Long-aged hard cheeses such as Parmigiano-Reggiano and Grana Padano (and also aged Gouda) can develop tyrosine crystals within the paste. Tyrosine is an amino acid released during proteolysis as casein breaks down during aging, and its low solubility makes it prone to crystallize.

item.title: Books I Read in 2024
item.description:
Favorites

  • Abroad in Japan
  • Who We Are and How We Got Here

English Books

Abroad in Japan

Chris Broad
I discovered Abroad in Japan nearly a year after my visit to Japan. While some videos seemed a bit too YouTubey for my taste, I found many to be genuinely entertaining and decided to give Chris Broad’s recent book a try. I didn’t expect much from a book by a YouTuber, but it turned out to be a delightful, light-hearted, and genuinely entertaining read. To be honest, I enjoyed it even more than Jonathan Clements’ A Brief History of Japan, which I read in preparation for my trip a year ago. I believe it’s worth a read even if you’ve never been to Japan or don’t plan to visit. The book is filled with humorous anecdotes, making it an effortless read that introduced me to a country and society that were completely foreign to me as a German. It manages to be both light-hearted and informative.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2024
item.description:
1. Bronze Age iron artifacts likely originated from meteorites, not from smelting terrestrial iron 🏆☄️.

    A geochemical approach using Fe:Co:Ni ratios can distinguish terrestrial from extraterrestrial iron. Modern iron and iron ores have distinct Fe:Co:Ni ratios compared to those found in Bronze Age artifacts.

  2. Caribbean pirates may have derailed an early U.S. attempt to adopt metric measures 📐🏴‍☠️.

    When the U.S. was considering standardizing measurements, French scientist Joseph Dombey set out to deliver a meter and a mass standard to Thomas Jefferson. British privateers intercepted Dombey in the Caribbean, leading to his capture and eventual death. The standards never reached Jefferson. Metric use later became legal in the U.S., but customary units remain common in everyday life.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2023
item.description:
More than two months into the new year, but better late than never, here is Things I Learned in 2023. This marks the fourth installment of my annual review, officially making it a series. As always, what follows are some surprising, entertaining, or enlightening things I stumbled upon in 2023.

  1. South Korea has a unique way of counting a person’s age 🇰🇷👴.

    In June 2023, South Korea adopted the international standard for calculating age in most legal and administrative contexts. Traditionally, many Koreans used “Korean age,” wherein a person was considered 1 year old at birth and gained an additional year on every New Year’s Day. Consequently, a baby born on Dec. 31 would be regarded as 2 years old the following day.

item.title: Books I Read in 2022
item.description: After a long drought in my 20s, I’m glad I got into reading more books again in 2022. The internet and YouTube, in particular, have such a strong pull that I almost have to force myself to take time and dedicate myself to reading something longer than an article. Also, I’m a terribly slow reader, which is just unbearable when I see people casually finishing a book in a couple of days. Still, I found great satisfaction in committing and extending my attention span beyond the instant rewards of today’s internet.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2021
item.description:
Introduction

Welcome to “Things I Learned in 2021”! For the second year now, here are noteworthy things that stood out to me last year.

  1. Hippocampal replay is a phenomenon observed in animals where sequences of cell activations in the hippocampus, a brain region associated with memory and spatial navigation, recur during sleep or awake rest at a much faster time scale 🧠🐈🐀⏰.

    Hippocampal replay is a phenomenon observed in animals where sequences of cell activations in the hippocampus, a brain region associated with memory and spatial navigation, recur during sleep at a much faster time scale than during the original activity. This behavior is exhibited by place cells, which fire in a sequence according to the animal’s movement path. The phenomenon has been observed in various animals and linked to memory consolidation. Studies have also found instances of preplay, where a sequence of activations occurs before the actual activity and replays in reverse.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2020
item.description:
In this blog post, I’ll share some of the interesting and unexpected things I came across on the internet in 2020. Without further ado, here are the 25 things that stood out to me.

  1. Brown is not a color, and there is no brown light 🟤🙅‍♂️🎨.

  2. The temperature and atmospheric pressure on Earth can vary greatly across its surface. However, there are lines around the Earth called isotherms and isobars along which the temperature and pressure, respectively, are the same. These lines are jagged in shape, and they intersect at two points, creating at least two points on Earth that have the exact same temperature and pressure at any given time 🌍.
